questions.stem: The SI unit of specific heat capacity is
questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin, so from $c = \frac{Q}{m\,\Delta\theta}$ the unit is joule divided by both kilogram and kelvin: $\text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$.

distractorRationale.a: This is the unit of heat capacity, which refers to a whole body rather than one kilogram
distractorRationale.c: This is the unit of specific latent heat, where no temperature change is involved
distractorRationale.d: Multiplies by mass and temperature instead of dividing, so the exponents are the wrong sign

questions.stem: The specific heat capacity of a substance is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of

options.text: 1 kg of the substance by 1 K
1 kg of the substance from 0 °C to 100 °C
1 kg of the substance without any change of temperature

questions.explanation: Specific heat capacity is defined per unit mass and per unit temperature rise, so it refers to exactly one kilogram and exactly one kelvin. This makes it a property of the material rather than of a particular object.

distractorRationale.a: That is the definition of heat capacity, which already includes the mass of the object
distractorRationale.c: That would be 100 times the specific heat capacity, not the quantity itself
distractorRationale.d: Heat supplied with no temperature change is latent heat, a separate quantity

questions.stem: Calculate the heat energy required to raise the temperature of 2.0 kg of water from 20 °C to 80 °C. Take the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg/K. Give your answer in joules.
questions.explanation: $Q = mc\,\Delta\theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times (80 - 20) = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504\,000\ \text{J}$. Use the temperature CHANGE of 60 K, not the final temperature of 80 °C.

questions.stem: Calculate the heat capacity of a block of aluminium of mass 0.50 kg, given that the specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/kg/K. Give your answer in joules per kelvin.
questions.explanation: Heat capacity $C = mc = 0.50 \times 900 = 450\ \text{J}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. This means 450 J raises the whole block by one kelvin, whereas 900 J would be needed for a full kilogram.

questions.stem: 4200 J of heat is supplied to 0.10 kg of water. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg/K, calculate the rise in temperature. Give your answer in kelvin.
questions.explanation: Rearranging $Q = mc\,\Delta\theta$ gives $\Delta\theta = \frac{Q}{mc} = \frac{4200}{0.10 \times 4200} = \frac{4200}{420} = 10\ \text{K}$. Because a change of 1 K equals a change of 1 °C, the rise could equally be quoted as 10 °C.

questions.stem: Water is used as the coolant in a car radiator mainly because it

options.text: has a very low specific heat capacity
has a very high specific heat capacity

questions.explanation: At 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹ water absorbs a great deal of heat for each degree its temperature rises, so a modest amount of water can carry away a large quantity of waste heat from the engine without itself becoming dangerously hot. It is also cheap and readily available.

distractorRationale.a: A low specific heat capacity would mean the coolant heated up rapidly and stopped absorbing heat effectively
distractorRationale.c: Water's fairly high boiling point of 100 °C is an advantage, and boiling easily would be a serious drawback
distractorRationale.d: Electrical conductivity has nothing to do with cooling, and in an engine it would be a hazard

questions.stem: 0.50 kg of water at 80 °C is mixed with 1.50 kg of water at 20 °C in a well-lagged container. Calculate the final temperature of the mixture. Give your answer in degrees Celsius.
questions.explanation: Heat lost equals heat gained, and the specific heat capacity cancels: $0.50(80 - \theta) = 1.50(\theta - 20)$. Expanding gives $40 - 0.50\theta = 1.50\theta - 30$, so $70 = 2.00\theta$ and $\theta = 35\ ^\circ\text{C}$. The result lies nearer 20 °C because there is three times as much cold water.

questions.stem: A body of mass 2.0 kg has a heat capacity of 1800 J/K. The specific heat capacity of the material of the body is
questions.explanation: Since $C = mc$, rearranging gives $c = \frac{C}{m} = \frac{1800}{2.0} = 900\ \text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. That value identifies the material as aluminium.

distractorRationale.a: Divided by 4 instead of 2, or divided twice by the mass
distractorRationale.c: Quoted the heat capacity itself, ignoring the mass
distractorRationale.d: Multiplied by the mass instead of dividing by it

questions.stem: An electric heater rated 840 W is used to heat 2.0 kg of water for 5.0 minutes. Assuming no heat is lost and taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg/K, calculate the rise in temperature of the water. Give your answer in kelvin.
questions.explanation: Heat supplied $= Pt = 840 \times (5.0 \times 60) = 840 \times 300 = 252\,000\ \text{J}$. Then $\Delta\theta = \frac{Q}{mc} = \frac{252\,000}{2.0 \times 4200} = \frac{252\,000}{8400} = 30\ \text{K}$. The time must be converted from minutes to seconds before use.

questions.stem: A metal block of mass 0.20 kg at 100 °C is dropped into 0.30 kg of water at 20 °C in a lagged calorimeter of negligible heat capacity. The final temperature of the mixture is 25 °C. Taking the specific heat capacity of water as 4200 J/kg/K, calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal. Give your answer in joules per kilogram per kelvin.
questions.explanation: Heat gained by the water $= 0.30 \times 4200 \times (25 - 20) = 6300\ \text{J}$. Heat lost by the metal $= 0.20 \times c \times (100 - 25) = 15c$. Setting them equal gives $15c = 6300$, so $c = 420\ \text{J}\,\text{kg}^{-1}\,\text{K}^{-1}$. The metal's temperature falls by 75 K while the water rises by only 5 K, which is why its specific heat capacity is so much smaller.
